issues.legal_issue: A reasonable doubt that a tenant was pressured by police into an eviction compromise can justify condoning delay in appealing the compromise decree.
material_facts: The tenants alleged that police pressure led them to enter into a compromise concerning the eviction proceedings.
A compromise had earlier been made at a police station and was addressed to a police officer before the eviction petition was filed.
The landlord’s complaint alleged that the lease document was forged and denied the landlord-tenant relationship, yet the landlord later sought eviction on that relationship.
The appellate court found the complaint and police-station compromise unrebutted and considered the allegation of coercion prima facie acceptable.
The tenants filed their appeal against the compromise decree 604 days late, and the appellate court accepted their explanation for the delay.
issues.conclusion: The delay in filing the appeal was properly condoned; the High Court’s order setting aside condonation was reversed, and the appellate court’s order was restored.
issues.legal_principle: Where there is reasonable doubt that police forced a party to enter into a compromise, the court process should weigh in favour of the party alleging that pressure. The Court relied on Ajad Singh v. Chatra (2005) 2 SCC 567, which treated a compromise recorded in a police station during pending litigation as a relevant circumstance warranting judicial scrutiny.

rule.if: appeal_from_rent_compromise_decree and delayed_appeal and coercion_alleged and reasonable_doubt_of_police_pressure

predicates.appeal_from_rent_compromise_decree: The proceeding is an appeal filed late against a compromise decree concerning eviction from rented premises.
predicates.delayed_appeal: The party filed the appeal after the applicable filing time had passed.
predicates.coercion_alleged: The appealing party said that police pressure caused it to enter into the compromise.
predicates.reasonable_doubt_of_police_pressure: Circumstances such as a compromise made at a police station, unrebutted evidence, or inconsistent positions by the other party raised reasonable doubt that police pressure caused the compromise.

issues.definition: When a party files a delayed appeal against a rent-related compromise decree and alleges police coercion supported by circumstances creating reasonable doubt, the delay is condoned.

issues.legal_issue: A compromise cannot support eviction of a tenant protected by rent-control law unless a statutory ground for eviction is made out.
material_facts: The landlord sought eviction under statutory grounds concerning alleged unauthorised transfer or subletting and a need for additional accommodation.
The parties filed a compromise, and the rent controller ordered the tenants to vacate and continue paying rent until they did so.
The compromise order did not identify any particular statutory ground for eviction or indicate that the court was satisfied such a ground existed.
The compromise terms recited in the order did not themselves establish a statutory ground for eviction.
issues.conclusion: A tenant cannot be evicted under the compromise order unless a statutory ground for eviction is made out; the order in this case did not record that any particular ground had been established.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sections 10(2)(ii)(a) and 10(3)(c) of the Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960, eviction may be ordered only when the prescribed ground is made out. A rent court cannot acquire authority to order eviction on a ground outside the statute merely because the parties consent. Under Order 23 Rule 3 of the Code of Civil Procedure, the court must satisfy itself that the compromise is lawful. K.K. Chari v. R.M. Seshadri considered Bahadur Singh v. Muni Subrat Dass, Kaushalya Devi v. Shri K.L. Bansal and Ferozi Lal Jain v. Man Mal. Nagindas Ramdas v. Dalpatram Ichharam held that if material before the court supports prima facie satisfaction of a statutory ground, that satisfaction may be presumed; such material may include clear admissions in the compromise, with judicial admissions under Section 58 of the Evidence Act standing as proof. The absence of a statutory ground also permits the decree’s invalidity to be raised in execution.

predicates.rent_control_eviction_proceeding: The proceeding concerns eviction of a tenant under a rent-control regime.
predicates.compromise_eviction_decree: The court ordered eviction on the basis of an agreement or compromise between the landlord and tenant.
predicates.no_material_supporting_statutory_ground: No evidence, admission, or other material before the court supported a statutory ground for eviction.

issues.definition: In a rent-control eviction proceeding, a compromise decree cannot authorize eviction when no material before the court supports a statutory ground for eviction.
